title: The ruling against Myanmar makes proving genocide more feasible | Kenneth Roth
html:
The international court of justice (ICJ) decision last Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya recognizes the plight of one of the world’s most persecuted minorities. It also resonates in Gaza, where the same court is now more likely to find that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians.

That possibility has incensed the Donald Trump administration, but it should think twice before attacking another international tribunal.

The case stems from the Myanmar military’s brutal “clearance operations” in 2017 when it used murder, torture, rape and arson to kill at least 10,000 Rohingya and to send more than 700,000 fleeing to neighboring Bangladesh. The Rohingya are a Muslim minority that has long faced severe discrimination in Myanmar, whose dominant Bamar ethnic group tends to be Buddhist and have lighter skin.

Myanmar has 135 recognized ethnic groups but refuses to accept the Rohingya as the 136th. A 1982 law denied most Rohingya citizenship despite their deep roots in the country.

Even Aung San Suu Kyi, awarded the Nobel peace prize in 1991 as an icon of her country’s quest for democracy, refused to call them Rohingya. She preferred the disparaging appellation “Bengali” to suggest they were foreigners who immigrated from Bangladesh. In 2019, she traveled to the Hague to defend the Myanmar military from the genocide charge.

Her actions reflected her fellow citizens’ vilification of the Rohingya. She also evidently hoped that by ingratiating herself with the military, it might allow her to become president despite a constitutional ban because her husband and two sons are British.

Instead, the military overthrew the country’s fledgling democracy in 2021 and has detained her ever since.

Genocide is defined in a widely ratified treaty. The Myanmar case, like many others, hinged on whether certain atrocities were committed with genocidal intent – that is, the intent to destroy a protected group, in this case a religious and ethnic minority, “in whole or in part”.

There was ample proof that the Myanmar army committed systematic murder, torture, rape, and arson against the Rohingya, but did it have the requisite intent?

In theory, genocidal intent can be proved by the statements of senior officials, but most are smart enough to use less incendiary language. As a result, intent usually must be inferred from conduct.

In rulings on genocide cases brought by Bosnia and Croatia against Serbia, the ICJ held in 2007 and 2015 that such a deduction could be made if “the only reasonable inference to be drawn from that conduct is one of genocidal intent”. That suggested to some that genocidal intent could not be found to coexist with another intent.

That view seemed built on genocides designed to kill a group “in whole”. For example, after a certain point during the Holocaust and the genocide in Rwanda, the aim was to kill every possible Jew or Tutsi.

But what about a genocide aimed at killing a group “in part”? That might arise when genocide is not the sole goal of mass atrocities but a means to another end, such as ethnic cleansing.

According to this interpretation, the ICJ’s Serbia rulings would perversely suggest that the commission of the crime against humanity of mass forced displacement might serve as a defense to allegations of genocidal intent. That made no sense.

In the Myanmar case, the court, by a vote of nine to six, interpreted this standard more sensibly. Citing general principles of criminal law, it ruled that dual intents were possible. “Genocidal intent may exist alongside other intentions, provided that such intentions are not incompatible with the existence of genocidal intent,” it explained.

In other words, its earlier ruling that genocidal intent must be shown to be the “only reasonable inference” from a course of conduct should not be read to mean that genocide is the sole intent. Rather, it meant there should be no reasonable understanding of the evidence that disproves genocidal intent, even if there was also a parallel intent.

The Myanmar government claimed its intent was not to commit genocide but to mount a counterinsurgency operation against a rebel group in the part of western Myanmar where most Rohingya lived. The court discounted that explanation because the army committed atrocities even in places where there was no insurgency and engaged in gratuitous atrocities such as raping women, killing children, burning villages and attacking fleeing civilians.

Myanmar also asked the court to consider the possibility, never admitted, that its aim was forced displacement, not genocide. That paralleled the ICJ’s finding from the evidence against Serbia that it did not have genocidal intent.

But in the latest case, the court held that so long as the only reasonable inference from the evidence was that Myanmar intended to commit genocide, it didn’t matter that the evidence reasonably supported the conclusion that Myanmar also sought to forcibly displace the Rohingya or to fight an insurgency. Genocide can be a means to an end, not just an end in itself.

That ruling must have sent shivers down the spines of Israeli officials. Anticipating it, Trump’s ambassador to the United Nations last month threatened the ICJ judges with sanctions akin to those already imposed on international criminal court judges if they “were to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide”. (The ICJ mainly resolves civil disputes between states, including on how to apply the Genocide Convention, while the ICC prosecutes individuals.)

But the ICJ didn’t lower the standard. It interpreted the standard in the most sensible way possible to ensure that the commission of parallel mass atrocities does not become a defense to genocide.

Moreover, as Trump toys with sanctions against yet another international court, does he really want to be seen as defending the brutal Myanmar military, which today is terrorizing people across Myanmar while ruthlessly quashing their hopes for democracy?

The administration of Joe Biden already found Myanmar to have committee genocide against the Rohingya. The Trump administration, having never repudiated that conclusion, says it is “examining” the ICJ ruling.

Like the Myanmar case, the genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel before the ICJ is likely to turn on the question of intent.

Similar to its Myanmar counterpart, the Israeli army gratuitously killed and harmed Palestinian civilians – indiscriminately bombing neighborhoods, attacking Hamas fighters knowing that there would be disproportionate civilian dead and wounded, shooting hungry Israelis as they ran for food, bombing housing blocks knowing many civilians remained inside, and creating conditions of starvation and deprivation that were incompatible with sustaining life.

The Israeli government didn’t attempt to kill all 2 million Palestinians in Gaza, just enough to persuade the rest to accept “voluntary emigration”, as an Israeli minister put it.

Might that attempted crime of mass forced deportation undermine an inference from these atrocities of genocidal intent? Similarly, might Israel’s military campaign against Hamas, however ruthless and indifferent to the requirements of international humanitarian law to spare civilians, serve a comparable role in negating genocidal intent?

The original ICJ language in the Serbia cases left open the possibility that this perverse “defense” might work. The Myanmar judgment makes clear it will not. The intent to commit genocide can coexist with the intent to forcibly displace or to fight an insurgency.

If the only reasonable conclusion from the totality of the evidence is that Israel possessed genocidal intent, which I suspect is true, the ICJ will find that Israel, like Myanmar, committed genocide.

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to take various remedial steps for the Rohingya, such as reparations, restoration of citizenship, the possibility of safe return to the country, and prosecution of offenders. But the court has no power to enforce its ruling. That task falls to the UN security council, which is likely to be stymied by China’s and Russia’s veto, and other governments, whose pressure so far has been ineffective.

But we should not minimize the importance to the Rohingya of the court’s acknowledgment of their plight. There was cheering among Rohingya in their refugee camps in Bangladesh. The odds now increase that the Palestinians of Gaza, too, will have their moment of recognition.

  • Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University, and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments
